title: MosaicKV: Serving Long-Context LLM with Dynamic Two-D KV Cache Compression
abstract: Long-context LLM services now sustain prompts with hundreds of thousands to millions of tokens, making the key-value (KV) cache a first-order serving cost. Because the cache grows linearly with context length, it can exhaust GPU memory, force smaller batches, and reduce serving throughput. Prior KV cache compression techniques typically target only the sequence dimension or only the channel dimension, which leaves limited headroom as context windows scale. Compressing both dimensions promises higher memory reduction, but applying the two forms of compression directly leads to significant accuracy loss. This paper introduces MosaicKV, a dynamic two-D (dimensional) KV cache compression system for extremely long-context serving. MosaicKV uses dynamic two-D compression to address the accuracy challenge, exploiting the non-uniform importance distribution of elements within the KV cache. Instead of applying one compression pattern globally, MosaicKV identifies important elements for each KV vector and selects compression strategies at the granularity of KV cache segments. To address the performance challenge, where fine-grained sparsity and compression management overhead can offset the gains from compression, MosaicKV introduces compressed KV cache management. This mechanism uses underutilized GPU and CPU resources to maintain compressed KV caches and accelerate attention computation. Evaluation on an H800 GPU with multiple LLMs shows that MosaicKV delivers up to 16x attention speedup, 4.8x lower decode latency, and 7.3x higher throughput than the uncompressed baseline. At the same time, it reduces memory usage by 3x and incurs only 1.76% average accuracy loss on LongBench and RULER.

title: What's Hidden Matters: Identifying Planning-Critical Occluded Agents using Vision-Language Models
abstract: Autonomous vehicles must safely navigate complex environments where planning-critical agents may be hidden from view. Current approaches often treat all occlusions with uniform conservatism, yielding needlessly defensive driving, or they infer hidden spaces without estimating the impact on the planner. This work bridges the critical gap between perception and planning by enabling Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to identify and reason about the specific hidden agents that are most critical to the ego-vehicle's trajectory. We introduce a novel framework that uses Planning KL-divergence (PKL), an information-theoretic metric, to systematically identify and rank occluded agents based on their impact on the ego vehicle's plan. Using this planning-aware ranking, we employ an expert VLM (GPT-5) to generate rich, structured annotations that capture the visual evidence and reasoning required for this task. We apply this framework to the nuScenes dataset to create a new benchmark focused on high-impact scenarios. We conduct comprehensive experiments on a wide range of general-purpose and domain-adapted VLMs, demonstrating that fine-tuning on our PKL-guided data yields dramatic performance improvements across all models. Notably, our results show that smaller, fine-tuned models significantly outperform their much larger zero-shot counterparts, and that our PKL-guided data selection strategy improves performance by approximately 30\% over random sampling. Our work presents the first systematic approach for training VLMs to focus on planning-critical occlusions, enabling more semantically grounded and efficient risk assessment in autonomous driving.

title: Booster Lab: A Data-Centric Pipeline for Learning Deployable Humanoid Locomotion Policies
abstract: Humanoid robot motion learning requires not only task-oriented control policies but also physically feasible and natural behaviors that can be transferred to real robots. However, robot-feasible motion data are often scarce: raw human demonstrations may be incompatible with the robot morphology, open-source clips vary in quality, and simulation-collected robot trajectories still require feasibility checking. To address these challenges, we propose a data-centric training and deployment pipeline that integrates motion data curation, real-to-sim model adaptation, AMP-based reinforcement learning, and sim-to-real deployment. We validate the framework on the Booster T1 robot and further provide preliminary cross-platform validation on Booster K1.

title: Review on Applications and Prospects of Federated Learning in New Power Systems
abstract: SignificanceAgainst the background of new power system development, massive amounts of multi-source heterogeneous data are distributed across multiple data owners. However, concerns regarding data ownership and privacy protection often lead to the formation of "data silos" among these owners. Meanwhile, electric power data, as critical information closely related to national security and economic development, has become a key production factor supporting the development of new power systems. As a distributed machine learning paradigm, federated learning enables multiple data owners to perform collaborative model training and data sharing while preserving data privacy, ensuring data security, and complying with regulatory requirements. Therefore, federated learning is of great significance for artificial intelligence modeling and data value mining in various application scenarios of new power systems.ProgressIn this context, this study conducted a systematic review of the recent applications of federated learning in new power systems, as well as the existing challenges and future research directions. First, the basic concepts, classifications, and application scenarios of federated learning were briefly introduced. According to the distribution of feature and sample spaces among different participants, federated learning can generally be categorized into horizontal federated learning, vertical federated learning, and federated transfer learning. Horizontal federated learning is applicable to scenarios in which participants share the same feature space but have different sample spaces. Vertical federated learning is suitable for scenarios in which participants share the same sample space but have different feature spaces. Federated transfer learning is applicable to scenarios with limited overlap in both the feature and sample spaces among participants. Subsequently, to address the secure data-sharing challenges faced by data owners in new power systems, the current applications of federated learning in various business scenarios were reviewed in detail. Specifically, the main application scenarios of horizontal federated learning include renewable energy generation and load forecasting, electricity consumption behavior analysis, power system cybersecurity, power network dispatch and optimization, and power network security and stability assessment. The primary application scenarios of vertical federated learning include the operation and control of distribution networks and microgrids, as well as vehicle-to-grid interaction and electric vehicles. Federated transfer learning has been mainly applied to load forecasting, power equipment fault diagnosis, regulation capability assessment of buildings, and power safety equipment inspection. At present, federated learning has been applied across nearly all fundamental components of new power systems. The review further indicates that, with increasing diversity of stakeholders in new power systems, selecting an appropriate federated learning framework requires comprehensive consideration of data characteristics, computational resources, privacy protection requirements, and application-specific demands. Consequently, customized federated learning solutions should be developed for different application scenarios. Furthermore, considering the characteristics of new power systems, including stringent real-time requirements, high standards for data privacy and security, and increasing demands for personalized services for business models, this study analyzed the major challenges facing federated learning applications. From the perspective of communication, practical large-scale deployment is hindered by heterogeneous computing resources, large model sizes, and numerous participating clients, resulting in reduced communication efficiency. From the perspective of privacy and security, although various encryption techniques have been adopted to protect data privacy, federated learning remains vulnerable to information leakage and malicious attacks, which affect its credibility and reliability. From the perspective of model training, the non-independent and identically distributed nature of data across participants, together with the emphasis of conventional federated learning on learning a single global model, often leads to poor training performance, limited model generalization, and difficulty in satisfying the personalized requirements of individual participants.Conclusions and ProspectsFinally, in view of the challenges facing federated learning, this study outlined three promising future research directions: hierarchical federated learning based on model compression and asynchronous update mechanisms, federated learning integrating blockchain and personalized differential privacy, and personalized federated learning based on client selection. These directions provide valuable references for data value mining in new power systems under the goals of "dual carbon". Although federated learning has great potential to promote the digital transformation of new power systems, its practical implementation and large-scale deployment still require effective solutions to challenges such as ensuring the stability of power communication networks, establishing a universal federated learning platform for power systems, and developing technical standards and specifications for federated learning in order to achieve its widespread application.

title: Approach of Product of Product Lines for Complex Aerospace Systems Development
abstract: As we often refer to term “System of Systems” (SoS) which encompasses multiple independent systems, similarly there of multiple Large and complex systems, such as aircraft which is made up of multiple intricate subsystems. Within an organization and/or across organizations, various development teams work on these subsystems, and each subsystem typically has its own product line to support different OEM requirements. However, the final decision on which Subsystem Configurations will be used is made at a higher system level. This creates a challenge where multiple product lines must be managed together, ensuring compatibility, consistency, and integration across the entire system, the traditional Product Line Engineering (PLE) approach is effective for managing configurations within an individual subsystem. However, when several subsystem product lines must work together within a broader system context, traditional PLE approaches fall short. Misalignment in interfaces, redundant functionalities, or inconsistent configuration decisions across teams can introduce integration delays and increase system complexity. Therefore, a new approach is needed to manage the collective behavior and coordination of these interconnected product lines. This paper explores these challenges and proposes a Product Line of Product Lines (PoPL) approach to systematically manage and coordinate multiple interconnected product lines in large-scale aerospace system development.

title: Effective Personalized AI Tutors via LLM-Guided Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Generative AI is reshaping work faster than education and training systems can adapt, creating an urgent need for efficient skill acquisition. Existing adaptive learning algorithms have limited visibility into learners’ progress, constraining their ability to personalize training effectively. We address this limitation by designing an AI-powered learning platform that integrates large language models (LLMs) with reinforcement learning (RL): the LLM generates exercises, provides tutoring support, and extracts rich behavioral signals from learner interactions, while the RL agent uses these signals to adaptively sequence practice question difficulty to maintain productive struggle matched to each learner’s evolving skill level. In partnership with the Taipei City Government and the American Institute in Taiwan, we launched a five-month “AI for Python Learning” program to evaluate this platform by conducting a randomized controlled trial (RCT) with 1,047 high school students. Despite a strong control condition that all students had access to an LLM tutor, the treatment group receiving additional RL-driven adaptive sequencing achieved a 0.15 standard deviation increase in in-person, paper-based exam performance—equivalent to 6–8 months of additional schooling. Mediation analysis suggests that these gains were driven by increased learner engagement. These results provide large-scale field evidence that combining rich interaction signals via LLM with adaptive learning algorithm can significantly accelerate skill acquisition beyond access to generative AI alone.
